# Introduction

@Dyer2017 examine trends in 10-K textual disclosure over the period 
1996–2013, documenting that annual reports filed with the U.S. Securities 
and Exchange Commission (SEC) have grown substantially longer, more 
standardized, and less specific over time. Using Latent Dirichlet 
Allocation (LDA), a natural language processing technique, they show that 
the median 10-K more than doubled in length from approximately 23,000 words 
in 1996 to nearly 50,000 words in 2013. They further document that this 
increase is largely driven by three specific disclosure topics: fair value 
and impairment disclosure following SFAS 157, internal control disclosure 
under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX), and risk factor disclosure mandated by 
the SEC in Item 1A.

Beyond the increase in length, @Dyer2017 document that 10-K filings have 
become more boilerplate, more redundant, and less readable over time, while 
specificity and the relative share of hard quantitative information have 
decreased. These trends have attracted considerable attention from 
regulators, investors, and standard setters, who have expressed concern 
about disclosure overload and the declining informativeness of corporate 
filings.

In this paper, we replicate and extend Figure 1, Panel A of @Dyer2017, 
which plots the distribution of 10-K word counts over time. Using a sample 
of 10-K filings from EDGAR covering the period 2000–2025, we show that the 
upward trend in 10-K length documented by @Dyer2017 has continued well 
beyond their sample period, with the median filing exceeding 60,000 words 
by 2025.

# Data and Sample Selection

```{python}
#| label: tbl-sample
#| tbl-cap: Sample description by year
#| output: asis
#| tbl-pos: H

table = summary[["year", "n_filings", "median_words"]].copy()
table.columns = ["Year", "N Filings", "Median Words"]
table["Year"] = table["Year"].astype(int)
table["Median Words"] = table["Median Words"].round(0).astype(int)

lines = [
    "\\begin{threeparttable}",
    "\\begin{tabular}{lrr}",
    "\\toprule",
    " & ".join(table.columns) + " \\\\",
    "\\midrule"
]
for row in table.itertuples(index=False):
    lines.append(f"{row[0]} & {row[1]:,} & {row[2]:,} \\\\")
lines += [
    "\\bottomrule",
    "\\end{tabular}",
    "\\begin{tablenotes}[flushleft]",
    "\\setlength{\\labelsep}{0pt}",
    "\\item \\emph{Note}: Sample covers 10-K filings from EDGAR, 2000--2025. "
    "Filings with fewer than 3,000 words and unsuccessful downloads are excluded. "
    "One filing per firm per year is retained (latest filing date).",
    "\\end{tablenotes}",
    "\\end{threeparttable}"
]
print("\n".join(lines))
```

## Design Choices

The replication follows @Dyer2017 as closely as the provided data allow.
The paper covers 1996–2013; our data extend from 2000 to 2025, which we 
treat as an extension. We exclude years before 2000 because fewer than 500 
filings are available per year in 1997–1999, making percentile estimates 
unreliable. Following the paper, we exclude filings with fewer than 3,000 
words and retain only successfully downloaded filings. Where a firm has 
multiple filings in the same fiscal year, we retain the latest filing by 
filing date.

Several exclusions from the original paper cannot be replicated. First, 
@Dyer2017 exclude amended filings (10-K/A), small business filings 
(10-KSB), and 10-K405 filings, but our dataset does not contain filing-type 
information that would allow us to implement these exclusions. Second, the 
paper excludes firms with negative market-to-book ratios, but Compustat data are not available in our dataset.

# Results

```{python}
#| label: fig-length
#| fig-cap: "10-K length over time. The figure plots the median, 25th, and 75th 
#|   percentile of word counts for 10-K filings by fiscal year, 2000–2025."
#| out-width: 95%

display(Image(filename="../output/fig1_panel_a.png"))
```

@fig-length replicates Figure 1, Panel A of @Dyer2017 and extends the 
sample through 2025. The median word count rises from approximately 25,000 words 
in 2000 to over 60,000 words in 2025, consistent with the trend documented in 
the paper. The 75th percentile exceeds 80,000 words by 2025, suggesting that 
longer filings have become increasingly common.

## Comparison with the Published Figure

Several differences from the original figure are worth noting. First, our sample 
starts in 2000 rather than 1996 due to insufficient EDGAR coverage in earlier 
years. Second, the word counts in our sample are consistently higher than those 
reported by @Dyer2017, which is expected given that the 10-K parsing method used 
to generate our data differs from the one used in the paper. Third, our figure 
shows a visible dip around 2008–2009, likely reflecting the financial crisis. 
Finally, our sample extends to 2025, showing that the upward trend documented 
by @Dyer2017 has continued well beyond their sample period.
